subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning a full module aiming for around 400-600 lines, using the toon kit (cel shading, fur edges, ink lines, anime eyes) imported from the toon kit path to build a Genshin Impact-style red panda standing on a mossy stone.

I'm working out the pose and layout — the panda balancing on all fours atop a rounded mossy boulder with its tail curved up for balance, scaling body proportions (stone footprint ~0.5m, panda length ~0.55m, tail ~0.45m) so the feet rest on the stone's top surface, and now sketching the skeleton hierarchy starting with the hips and spine chain running from hips through chest toward the neck and head.

Defining the spine chain...

Now I'm choosing the red panda's color palette: rust-orange coat with lighter highlights, dark brown-black belly and legs, cream facial markings, and alternating orange/dark rings on the tail, applying cel-shaded paints with a fur edge effect to countershade the dark underside against the body.

I'm sketching the head design next — a round shape with big cheek tufts, cream muzzle, triangular ears with cream rims, dark tear-line markings, a black nose, and anime-style eyes via decal, built as a scaled sphere jointed at the neck.

Now I'm planning the neck as a short two-joint chain since red pandas barely have necks, placing the joints just above the chest and defining a curved path between them.

I'm also figuring out the head joint position and orientation, parenting it to the neck's last spine joint, and setting up local axis words (forward, up, right) to position the head slightly forward and up from its joint.

For the skull shape, I'm adding a sphere part scaled to a head-like proportion, offset forward and up from the head bone origin.

For the decals, I'm planning to get the skull's surface and project eye decals onto it using the local head coordinates, with the direction vector angled outward based on the mirror sign so left and right eyes work symmetrically.

Now I'm scaling the eye decal size relative to the head proportions and computing the actual z-depth on the skull ellipsoid at the chosen x,y offset so the eyes sit flush against the curved surface.

I'm also checking whether the muzzle shape, positioned below and forward of the eyes, might overlap and cover part of the eye decal, since their vertical spans appear close.

So I'll nudge the eyes slightly further outward and bump up eye size a bit for that cute, big-eyed anime panda look. Now I'm thinking about the white cheek ruffs characteristic of red pandas, planning to build pointed tufts using cones or spikes arranged around the sides of the skull.

Still writing tuft placement...

For ears, I'm planning a rounded-triangle extrude shape, orange outside with cream-white rim and inner, pointing up and outward.

Refining the ear outline shape...

Now I'm planning the facial markings: white patches above the eyes, a cream muzzle and cheeks, and dark tear marks running from eye to mouth corner. I'll build these as separate pieces — a muzzle sphere, cheek tufts, brow patches as small cones or ellipses, and tear lines as painted sweeps — using head-local coordinates to position them relative to a fixed head center.

Adding brow spots and dark tear-mark stripes using distance-to-segment math, since real red pandas have rust-colored tear lines below their eyes -- a nice identity cue worth including in the cel-shaded head paint function.

I'm defining the color palette: warm orange, cream, dark brown for legs, rust for tail rings. Then setting up the coat shading with cel-shaded fur edges, darkening the belly based on downward-facing normals to simulate the underside shadow.

For the legs, I'm chaining joint positions from shoulder to foot for both front and hind limbs, keeping them tucked under the body but slightly spread for balance, and positioning feet onto the stone's surface. I'm also shaping the stone itself as a lathed profile with a flat-ish domed plateau and bulging sides for the panda to perch on.

I want to make the stone blocky and faceted rather than smooth, then paint it with mossy patches on upward-facing surfaces using a jagged cel-shaded edge transitioning to blue-gray stone below. I'm considering adding a few flattened-sphere moss clumps and maybe small glowing flowers or crystal accents for that stylized Genshin look.

Now I'm working out the panda's foot placement relative to the stone's domed top, adjusting the lathe profile so there's a flat plateau around radius 0.26 at height 0.30 where the feet can rest before the surface curves down.

I'm reconsidering the stone proportions relative to the panda's body so the balancing pose reads naturally, keeping all four feet on the plateau with the tail raised. Now I'm working out the leg chains from hip to paw, treating each paw as a flattened rounded shape attached at the ankle rather than part of the main limb chain.

Still working out limb proportions...

Front legs get two segments with elbow bending back, named shoulder/elbow/hand; hind legs get three segments with hip/knee/ankle bends and a foot tip. I'm setting left-side legs to positive X, parenting front legs to the chest joint and hind legs to the hips, tapering thigh radius from 0.06 to 0.04, and giving the fur a dark color.

For leg coloring I'm applying a vertical gradient shading from rust-orange at the top to dark near the paws, matching red panda coloring where the lower legs turn black, and checking that the limb function returns point arrays compatible with the chain builder for drawing the polyline paths.

Now I'm positioning the hip and shoulder joints for a wide, balanced stance—front legs angled slightly outward and hind legs similarly spread—then planning a long bushy ringed tail raised up behind the body.

Writing tail chain code...

I'll keep the tail geometry smooth rather than faceted, and set up the hip-to-tail parenting chain. For the head, I'm defining a jaw joint parented to the head, aimed forward, with a small cream-colored lower jaw mesh to form the mouth.

I'm adding a rounded black nose sphere at the muzzle front, then sketching thin dark curves for the mouth line draped onto the muzzle surface using a catmull sweep.

Mapping the mouth lines as a drooping 'w' shape below the nose, working out left and right drape paths in head-local coordinates relative to the muzzle surface.

Below that, I'm placing a separate lower jaw in cream, positioning cheek ruffs and eyes, and planning the forehead patch in orange with cream brow spots, then starting to define head cel-paint regions relative to the head's coordinate frame.

For coloring, I'll make the lower skull region cream with a zigzag boundary to mimic red panda cheek fur, keeping it separate from the muzzle cream, and add a cream brow patch defined by a dz/dx range above the eyes.

I need to carefully position the brow spot ellipse so it doesn't overlap the eye decal — shifting the eye center up slightly so the brow sits cleanly above it. I'm also adding a dark rust tear mark running from near the eye down along a short segment, drawn even over the cream region.

For the rest of the body, I'm keeping ears orange with a cream inner rim, skipping a cream chest bib, and scattering small low-poly cone spikes along the back as fur tufts using a filtered placement so they stay off the belly area.

I'll scatter these spikes along the body and haunches, add a few on the tail, then layer in whiskers as thin cream-colored rods from the muzzle sides. For the stone, I'm planning moss tufts using textured cards scattered across the upper surface where the normal faces upward.

Adding a handful of small daisy-style flower cards near the rim for detail, maybe with a subtle glow, though I need to watch for glow breaking on card materials.

For the stone, I'm setting up a cel-shaded blue-grey rock palette with mossy green patches using a fur-edge technique driven by surface normals, so flat tops stay mossy while sides get a toothed moss/stone boundary, finished off with an ink outline for that cartoon look.

I'll add subtle darker crack lines across the stone surface using cellular noise, and mottle the moss with two shades of green for texture variation. For the shape, I'm going with a faceted low-poly lathe profile, and considering adding one smaller companion rock at the base to round things out.

Now I'm thinking through the rigging: the stone needs to attach somewhere in the joint hierarchy. Since hips is the root, I'm weighing whether to make the stone a child joint under hips or give it its own separate root, since a second root would break the structure.

For the eye color, I'm deciding on an iris shade that gives good contrast without clashing with the overall palette.

For the decal placement on the skull, I'm working out the surface attachment, mirroring for the left/right eyes, and the direction vector for positioning each eye correctly on the face.

I'm also checking the ear placement math, confirming they sit at the right position relative to the skull's bounds so they're embedded naturally at the top of the head rather than floating outside the outline.

For the ear geometry itself, I'm mirroring the extrusion for left and right sides by flipping the x-axis scale, with the cross product determining thickness orientation so the ears stay symmetric. The cream inner coloring faces forward toward the camera, matching how the ear would actually be visible on a red panda.

Now I'm working out the inner ear detail as a scaled-down outline relative to the ear's centroid, deciding to skip the darker ear-back shading and tip fringing for simplicity, and keeping the overall color palette lean since cel-shaded paints don't add to the count. I'm starting to lay out the spine path using a catmull-rom curve rooted at the hips.

Checking the body height proportions against the ground, I realize the panda should sit lower for a stouter look, so I'm adjusting the belly height and leg segment lengths to keep the short, chunky limbs properly reaching the ground when bent.

Legs emerge inset within the body so the offset works fine, and paws sink slightly into the stone base without causing floor clipping issues. Checking overall proportions: total height comes to roughly 1.0m including the 0.3m stone base, with the tail raised as the tallest point — a stylized but reasonable scale compared to a real red panda's 0.6m length.

Now reconsidering the tail length since my initial path was too long relative to the body; I'm recalculating shorter waypoints for the tail curve starting from the hips and curving upward, aiming for a more proportional ~0.6-0.7m length instead of the exaggerated 0.95m.

Refining the tail radius formula...

I'm deciding to keep the coat simple with a flat orange body tone rather than adding a separate dorsal stripe, then moving on to the paws—adding small toe spheres with claws and a dark flat color for the paw pads.

For the limb chains I'm using the root-elbow-tip structure so each leg has three named joints, attaching parts to the chain's tip bone, and skipping separate digit joints since toes can just be parts on the foot bone. I'm tagging the front chains with an "arm" role and the hind chains with a "leg" role.

Now I'm working out the head and neck setup: the neck chain spans two segments with two names (no extra tip joint), and the head joint parents off the last neck joint with its own direction and role.

I'm introducing a scale constant H (set to 1.1 for a slightly larger, cuter head) and building local helper functions to convert left/up/forward offsets into scaled model coordinates, keeping the neck endpoint unscaled while applying H to head dimensions and paint calculations.

Now I'm starting the actual implementation, importing the needed functions from the builder library and its toon/glow kits, and confirming all these utilities come from the same module.

I'm defining the scene metadata plus core measurements and color constants for the red panda model, then setting up toon-shaded material cels for each body region like orange fur, cream highlights, and dark shadows...

Writing fur edge function...

Adding the stone cell pattern and moss edging...

I'm thinking through the tooth direction on the fur edge so it zigzags correctly along the stone ring, then moving on to defining a tuft helper function for scattering fur across the surface.

Now I'm scattering fur spikes across the body sweep, filtering hit points by their normal direction, and computing each spike's direction as a blend between a backward-up vector and the surface normal, keeping the coat color consistent with the cel paint pattern.

For the cheek tufts, I'm setting up a surface sampler around a skull reference point and placing a few symmetric tufts at specific azimuth/elevation angles on each side of the head.

I'll add small rust crest tufts between the ears, then move to the ear shapes themselves. For the lathe-generated body parts, I'm defining a rotated profile with sharp creases at corners over 35 degrees and smooth elsewhere, aiming for a faceted, stone-like surface rather than smooth geometry.

Now I'm adding small boulder details using flattened icosahedron geometry placed at the base, checking they sit outside the main stone's radius without clipping through, and centering the stone's position relative to the panda's feet. Writing moss tufts texture code...

Still scattering cards...

I'm also considering adding a carved glowing rune decal on the stone's front face for a bit of magical flavor, applying it with a decal function and testing its orientation on the stone surface around the mid-height.

Skipping whiskers as rods and simplifying the jaw to a basic lower-jaw sphere without teeth or tongue, with the muzzle attached to the head bone. Now I'm setting up the builder and starting the joint hierarchy, beginning with the hips as the root joint and building out the spine chain from there.

Writing more joint chain code...

Checking neck sweep radius and body overlap confirms the front joins cleanly at z=0.32. Comparing head and body heights, the head sits slightly above the back which seems fine, so I'm adjusting the neck joint height to BY+0.06 to keep proportions balanced.

Now I'm defining the skull geometry as a faceted sphere sized and positioned relative to the head joint, using low-poly segments for the cel-shaded style.

Placing the nose sphere just forward of the muzzle so it pokes out slightly, then working out the mouth drape path with curved points across the muzzle surface for a natural mouth line.

Adding the jaw joint and a small cream sphere for the lower jaw shape, then placing a tiny pink tongue part just above it inside the mouth.

Now I'm adding thin whisker rods extending outward from the muzzle on each side, then moving on to defining the ear outline points for the ear shape construction.

Computing inner ear placement...

I'll keep the ear coloring simple: orange outer with cream inner, skipping extra detail at the base. Then I'm adding cheek tufts in cream, considering a chest bib patch but deciding to skip it, and setting up dorsal rust-colored stripe sectors along the spine.

Now I'm building the leg geometry, starting with hind leg hip and foot positions for both left and right sides using mirrored coordinates...

Adjusting the leg radius taper for a thigh bulge, then placing the paw as an ellipsoid at the foot tip with three toe spheres positioned slightly forward and offset for a natural splay.

I'm adding tiny forward-pointing claw cones in cream color using a spike helper, and setting the paw color to dark. Then I'm defining the front legs with shoulder-to-hand limb geometry, parented to the spine for the arm role.

For the front paw placement, chest region, and balance details like the curved tail and spread forelegs, I'm using the hips bone for all stone-related parts so that scattered surface hits automatically inherit it, and planning fur tuft spikes with skin weighting plus the total part count for legs and paws.

Tallying up the remaining pieces — toes, claws, head details, ears, tufts, whiskers, and tail — brings the count to roughly 150. I want to add a cream chest bib, a tail tip tuft, red panda-style ears, a forehead crest with small spikes, and tiny brow fluff tufts above each eye. No special rig pose is needed for the jaw, so I'll finalize by making sure the function returns the root properly.

Now I'm setting up the rune decal on the stone surface, positioning it using the lathe geometry's curved profile and adding a glow effect to make it stand out, while checking that the stone's front surface coordinates line up correctly for placement.

Trying to work out the lathe's angular convention for front-facing vs back-facing on the default upright axis — with 36° steps and 0 pointing back, a vertex would land at front if spin is 0, so I'll set spin to 18 to center a flat face there instead, accepting some uncertainty in the result. Now I'm sketching the rune texture SVG with a circle and glyph shapes.

Still writing SVGs for the daisy petals and moss tuft, then setting up the stone surface scattering logic with moss card hits carrying bone references for lean, bend, and sink variation.

I confirm the scale parameter exists in the stick function signature alongside embed, flow, spin, bone, and group options. Now I'm writing the head paint function, defining facial coordinates relative to the head joint and starting to mask out a tear-drop shaped region using a distance function.

Still writing paint logic...

Thinking through the cheek coloring—since cheek tufts should be cream, I want to restrict the lower cream region appropriately without accidentally coloring the back of the head, so I'm adjusting the z-depth threshold.

I'm also checking the tear-streak placement relative to the eye position, muzzle boundary, and segment distance function so the streak sits correctly on the cheek without overlapping the muzzle too much.

Now I'm thinking through how the cel-shaded paint system resolves colors based on lighting direction, and considering texel density across the paint sheet given the model's scale and the default texture resolution.

I'm bumping paintSize to 2048 for crisper toon edges and checking that the atlas stays manageable alongside other textures. Writing tail ring pattern code...

Checking proportions next: ring widths, paw-to-stone contact height, overall silhouette top-to-bottom to make sure nothing clips the ground plane.

Now working out tuft placement along the tail, deciding to skip scattered spikes mid-tail and instead focus a small cluster of spikes near the tail tip, oriented using a ring of points around the tail's end frame.

Still defining parts...

I'll reuse the coat color for body and neck continuity, keep haunch ellipsoids in the same tone, and skip the cream chest bib since it'd be hidden behind the neck anyway. For the moss and daisy cards, I'll leave them untinted so their own textures show through, and I'll wrap the daisy card meshes with a glow effect.

For daisy placement, I'm scattering hits along the rim using a filtered normal range to avoid overlap with the panda's feet, and parenting the hind leg chain to the hips for proper articulation. I'm working out toe positions on the paw by offsetting from the paw center along x and z.

Now I'm positioning the hind paws relative to the ankle, placing toes slightly forward, and starting to define the eye with an iris color.

I'm working out the spike offset signature for the cheek details, using direction vectors and skull anchor points to place cheek tufts with specific outward-facing directions for each side.

I'm planning the crest tufts along the skull top, pointing upward and back with slight azimuth spread, colored orange, and then moving on to scatter fine fur across the body before writing the final code.
